### Question 1

Eupnea is the reference point everything else is measured against: quiet, even, and requiring no visible effort. A helpful anchor is that a resting adult moves roughly half a liter of air per breath, and doing that a dozen or so times a minute covers normal metabolism. Notice that published ranges differ a little (12 to 18 versus 12 to 20) because they are conventions, not physical constants, so what matters clinically is the trend for that individual rather than a single cutoff. Every other term in this topic is simply a description of how a pattern departs from eupnea: faster, slower, deeper, or irregular.

### Question 2

The prefix 'tachy-' means fast, the same root as in tachycardia and in a car's tachometer. So tachypnea is a statement about frequency only. The trap on exams is dyspnea, which is not a number at all: it is a symptom the person experiences and reports, and someone can be dyspneic at a rate of 16 or comfortable at a rate of 26. Hyperpnea is a third, independent dimension, describing how much air moves per breath. Keeping frequency, volume, and the person's report in separate mental columns prevents most terminology errors in this topic.

### Question 3

Fix your attention on one landmark, such as the chest rising, and count each time that landmark repeats. The in-and-out together is a single event, the same way one swing of a pendulum includes the return trip. Students most often inflate the count by unconsciously registering both the rise and the fall, which turns a rate of 16 into a reported 32 and triggers an unnecessary escalation. If the chest is hard to see, watching the abdomen or resting a hand lightly on it counts the same cycles.

### Question 4

The body regulates breathing primarily around waste removal, not fuel supply. Carbon dioxide is the waste, and because it forms carbonic acid in solution, a small rise in it produces a measurable pH change that the brainstem sensors read almost instantly. Oxygen sensors in the carotid and aortic bodies exist, but they stay relatively quiet until oxygen drops a long way. A striking demonstration of this hierarchy is why hyperventilating before an underwater breath-hold is dangerous: it washes out carbon dioxide and silences the urge to breathe while oxygen keeps falling, so a person can lose consciousness before ever feeling air hunger.

### Question 5

Respiration is the one routine vital sign the person can consciously override. You can hold your breath; you cannot hold your heartbeat or your temperature. That dual control creates a genuine observer effect: the act of measuring changes what is measured. The practical workaround is to keep your fingers on the radial pulse after you finish counting it and shift your gaze to the chest, so the person assumes the pulse count is still underway. Attention to this matters because a self-conscious count that reads 14 can mask a true resting rate of 24.

### Question 6

Minute ventilation, the total air moved per minute, is rate multiplied by tidal volume, so the body has two independent levers to pull. Tachypnea is pulling the rate lever; hyperpnea is pulling the volume lever. Recognizing which lever moved is diagnostically useful: healthy exercise typically raises depth first, while pain, fever, anxiety, and stiff or restricted lungs tend to produce many small breaths instead. Two people can have identical minute ventilation with completely different patterns and completely different underlying problems.

### Question 7

Tidal volume runs about 6 to 8 mL per kilogram at any age, so a 3.5 kg newborn moves roughly 25 mL of air per breath against an adult's 500 mL. Meanwhile the newborn burns oxygen faster per unit of body mass. With a small fixed volume per breath and a large demand, the only remaining variable is frequency, which is why 40 breaths a minute is unremarkable in a newborn and alarming in an adult. Rates decline steadily through childhood as tidal volume grows, reaching adult values around adolescence.

### Question 8

Opioids act on the same medullary centers that read carbon dioxide, raising the threshold at which rising carbon dioxide triggers a breath, so the person simply feels less push to breathe. The result is a slow but otherwise unremarkable-looking pattern, which is part of why it is easy to miss. Note the ordering of clues: the rate falls before oxygen saturation does, and supplemental oxygen can keep saturation looking normal while ventilation deteriorates. Reserve the word apnea for actual cessation, since the two findings carry different urgency.

### Question 9

Carbon dioxide dissolved in blood forms carbonic acid, so exhaling it removes acid. When metabolism floods the blood with ketoacids, the lungs are the fastest lever the body has, capable of responding within minutes, while the kidneys take hours to days. The clinical implication is that the dramatic breathing is the rescue effort rather than the emergency itself, and suppressing it would make the acidosis worse. It also explains a hazard: if that person tires and their ventilation falls, pH can drop sharply because the compensation has been withdrawn.

### Question 10

Multiplying a short sample is a shortcut that works only when the underlying process is uniform, and irregularity is precisely the violation of that condition. Consider a pattern of six breaths followed by a 15-second pause: one window yields 24 and the next yields zero, from the same person a few seconds apart. Because the direction of error is unknowable in advance, no correction factor can rescue the shortcut. The additional 45 seconds also gives you something the number alone cannot capture, namely the shape of the pattern, which is often the more informative finding.

### Question 11

Both patterns pair breathing with pauses, so the distinguishing feature is the shape of the envelope: gradual and wave-like versus abrupt and switch-like. That shape maps onto mechanism. Cheyne-Stokes reflects an unstable feedback loop, in which delayed circulation time means the brainstem is always responding to carbon dioxide readings that are already out of date, producing overshoot and undershoot. Biot reflects direct damage to, or suppression of, the brainstem rhythm generator itself, so the output starts and stops without a ramp. Describing what you actually see, rather than reaching for the label first, keeps that distinction usable at the bedside.

### Question 12

Two things make saturation a lagging indicator. First, compensation: raising the rate can hold gas exchange steady while the underlying problem worsens beneath a normal-looking number. Second, the shape of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve, which is nearly flat at the top, so arterial oxygen can fall a long way, from about 100 down to 60 mmHg, while saturation slips only from roughly 100 percent to 90 percent, and then drops steeply once that reserve is spent. By the time the oximeter looks bad, the compensation has already failed. That is why a carefully counted rate, rather than an eyeballed one, is often the first hard evidence of trouble.
